title: Place Value Worksheets: Tens and Ones Expanded Form
intro: A ten is one group of ten ones. Use that group to explain why the two digits in a number have different values.
html:
One ten is ten ones

Count 23 small objects. Move ten into one group, then ten into another group. Three objects remain. You still have 23 objects: two tens and three ones.

23 = 20 + 3

Two groups of ten have a value of 20. The three remaining ones have a value of 3.

Connect the groups to the digits

The 2 in 23 tells how many tens there are. It does not mean two individual objects. The 3 tells how many ones remain. Ask the child to point to the two groups and then the three loose objects while saying “two tens and three ones.”

If the child writes 2 + 3: ask how many objects are inside each group. Count one group together and label it 10. Two groups make 20, so the sum is 20 + 3.

Teen numbers have one ten

For 16, make one group of ten and leave six ones. Write 16 = 10 + 6. Keep the group intact while counting the remaining six. Then open the group and recount to check that grouping did not add or remove objects.

A zero means no loose ones

For 40, make four groups of ten with no objects left over. You can write 40 + 0. The answer key omits zero terms, so it shows 40. Both represent four tens and no ones. Keep the zero when writing the ordinary numeral 40; writing 4 describes a different quantity.

Read the sum back into a number

After writing 50 + 7 for 57, cover the original number. Ask how many tens and ones the sum describes. Five tens and seven ones rebuild 57. Do not count the groups as if each group were only one object.

Use this page after grouping practice

Each set shows six distinct numerals from 10 through 99. Children write the tens value plus the ones value. The printable uses numerals rather than pictures of bundles; provide objects or base-ten blocks when the child still needs a physical model. A set does not guarantee a teen number or a zero ones digit.

The answer key gives expanded forms such as 60 + 4. An explicit zero term and a reversed sum such as 4 + 60 are mathematically valid. Ask the child to explain which term represents the tens.
